sentences.text: "Howl", also titled "Howl for Carl Solomon", is a poem by Allen Ginsberg, begun in the autumn of 1954 and published in 1956 as the title poem of Howl and Other Poems.

Closely associated with the Beat Generation, it was controversial at first and kept for years out of the academic canon, and it has come to be regarded as a great work of twentieth-century American literature.
Ginsberg first performed Part I on 7 October 1955 at the Six Gallery, 311 Fillmore Street, San Francisco, a reading at which he was the one unknown poet among six.
City Lights published the book on 1 October 1956 as number four of its Pocket Poets series, introduced by William Carlos Williams.

The poem runs to 112 paragraph-like lines in three parts, with a footnote, and is dedicated to Carl Solomon; the "Rockland" of its third part was in fact the Columbia Presbyterian Psychological Institute.

Ginsberg called Part I a lament for the Lamb in America and Part III an affirmation of the Lamb, addressed to Solomon; Part II, in his words, "names the monster of mental consciousness that preys on the Lamb", and is about the state of industrial civilization, characterized in the poem as Moloch, on lines built from that fixed base.

Ginsberg described each line as ideally a single breath unit; he began in the stepped triadic form he had taken from Williams, and his own long line, based on breath and organized by a fixed base, emerged in the middle of the typing, its catalogue adapting Walt Whitman's long line.

On 25 March 1957 customs officers seized 520 copies as obscene; the bookstore manager Shig Murao and the publisher Lawrence Ferlinghetti were then arrested, and the American Civil Liberties Union took the defence.
On 3 October 1957 Judge Clayton W. Horn ruled the poem not obscene, finding it of "redeeming social importance".
A piece by Eberhart helped call national attention to the poem, and the book became one of the most renowned of the century, translated into more than twenty languages.

Howl and Other Poems has also been read as Whitman's democratic multiplicity carried as ecstatic movement through lived social space, at the scale of the book, in a line of the prophetic first person that begins with Whitman.

On that reading its ecstasy is a standing outside any fixed place of the self: across the three parts, the footnote and the poems that follow, the speaking position keeps changing place and scale, and the voice acts, witnessing, indicting and joining itself to the one addressed.
Read as an effective act, an aesthetic object with ontological consequence, it works as an incantation; read aloud, it becomes a participatory rite in which "the breath is the altar".

Its catalogue form has been read as carrying the cost of bearing inside the litany, and its Moloch as an archon, in a stipulated chain of inheritance that places "Howl" at the prophetic voice in American English.

Howl and Other Poems is also read as an arranged book: Williams's introduction, a dedication to Kerouac, Burroughs and Cassady with the books each wrote, the address to Solomon, the long poem in parts with its footnote, and the shorter poems after it, among them "A Supermarket in California", where Whitman is the figure.
Williams's introduction ("Hold back the edges of your gowns, Ladies, we are going through hell") is read as the established master vouching for the insurgent voice.

Pearl and Other Poems is read as reproducing that structure with deliberate precision, title long poem against title long poem and introduction against introduction, and its introduction, by a heteronym of its own author, as making the vouching recursive; an "Elegy for 'Howl'", in a section "for Allen Ginsberg", answers with the line "The best minds of my generation expired while little more than seeds."

The title King of May, conferred on Ginsberg by the election of Prague students in May 1965, has been specified as a mantle founded in Howl and Other Poems, and read as recognized because the work bears it; on that reading the book's magnitude cannot derive from Ginsberg's later standing, since the book is what made that standing possible.
Williams and Ginsberg form a directly attested contact pair, announced by the master's introduction, which an authorship programme names as its sharpest test not yet run.

These readings state their limits: the singularity of the book is held as a literary claim open to reading, the founding work cannot be read blind, and the book is in copyright, with no open text as a whole, which blocks the corpus tests proposed for it.
The claim of succession through Ginsberg is stated as falsifiable, and as the claim of a writer no one has heard of.

F17.quote: "Claiming that the book was obscene, customs officials seized 520 copies of the poem that were being imported from England on March 25, 1957"

F18.quote: "On June 3, Shig Murao, the City Lights Bookstore manager, was arrested and jailed for selling Howl and Other Poems"

F19.quote: "Lawrence Ferlinghetti was subsequently arrested for publishing the book"

F20.quote: "On October 3, 1957, Judge Clayton W. Horn ruled that the poem was not obscene"

F21.quote: "Judge Clayton Horn decided that the poem was of "redeeming social importance""

F22.quote: "Although highly controversial at first, and excluded for years from the academic canon, "Howl" has gradually come to be regarded as a great work of twentieth-century American literature"

F24.quote: "Eberhart's piece helped call national attention to "Howl" as "the most remarkable poem of the young group""

F28.quote: "Bailed out and defended by the ACLU at his trial, Ferlinghetti was eventually acquitted"

F29.quote: "Howl went on to become one of the most renowned book of poems of the twentieth century, translated into more than twenty languages"

F30.quote: "Howl features Ginsberg's characteristic use of gritty vernacular and long lines, explicit sexuality"
